options.a: A loose layer of food debris and dead epithelial cells on the tooth surface
options.b: A structured microbial community embedded in an extracellular matrix on teeth
options.c: The acquired pellicle, a bacteria-free salivary protein film coating the enamel
options.d: Mineralized calculus deposits formed from calcium phosphate on the teeth

distractorExplanations.a: That describes food debris and materia alba; biofilm is an organized microbial community bound in a matrix.
distractorExplanations.c: The pellicle is the acellular salivary glycoprotein film that forms first; biofilm develops on it once bacteria colonize.
distractorExplanations.d: Calculus is mineralized biofilm; the biofilm itself is an unmineralized, living microbial community.

options.a: Breaking down salivary proteins into ammonia
options.b: Releasing endotoxins that inflame the gingiva
options.c: Invading the pulp through intact enamel tubules
options.d: Producing acid from fermentable carbohydrates

distractorExplanations.a: Ammonia production (for example arginine metabolism by other species) raises plaque pH; S. mutans lowers it with acid.
distractorExplanations.b: Endotoxin (LPS) comes from gram-negative periodontal pathogens; S. mutans is gram-positive and cariogenic through acid.
distractorExplanations.c: Enamel has no tubules and S. mutans demineralizes the surface with acid; tubules are a feature of dentin.

options.a: Supporting the tooth, sensory input, and nutrient supply to cementum/bone interface
options.b: Forming enamel and dentin matrix during tooth development and eruption
options.c: Sealing the sulcus base by attaching gingival epithelium to enamel
options.d: Anchoring the gingiva to the alveolar crest through the free gingival fibers

distractorExplanations.b: Enamel is formed by ameloblasts and dentin by odontoblasts; the PDL supports and nourishes the erupted tooth.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the junctional epithelium's role; the PDL's principal fibers attach cementum to alveolar bone.
distractorExplanations.d: Gingival fiber groups support the gingiva; the PDL attaches root to bone and adds proprioception and nutrition.

options.a: Mainly forming fluorapatite during tooth development before eruption
options.b: Enhancing remineralization and inhibiting demineralization/bacterial enzymes
options.c: Killing cariogenic bacteria outright at the levels found in toothpaste
options.d: Raising plaque pH by buffering acids produced after sugar intake

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-eruptive systemic uptake is now considered a minor effect; fluoride's main benefit is topical and post-eruptive.
distractorExplanations.c: At toothpaste levels fluoride inhibits bacterial enzymes such as enolase but does not sterilize plaque.
distractorExplanations.d: Acid buffering is the job of salivary bicarbonate and phosphate; fluoride works through remineralization and enzyme inhibition.

options.a: Triggering IgE-mediated allergic reactions
options.b: Digesting starches before they reach the stomach
options.c: Buffering plaque acid after carbohydrate intake
options.d: Mucosal immune defense against oral microbes

distractorExplanations.a: Allergy and anaphylaxis are IgE-mediated; secretory IgA blocks microbial adherence on mucosal surfaces.
distractorExplanations.b: Starch digestion in the mouth is done by salivary amylase, an enzyme, not by an immunoglobulin.
distractorExplanations.c: Acid buffering is done by bicarbonate and phosphate in saliva; IgA is an antibody, not a buffer.

options.a: Maxillary central incisor (around age 6)
options.b: Mandibular first molar (around age 6)
options.c: Mandibular second molar (around age 12)
options.d: Maxillary first premolar (around age 10)

distractorExplanations.a: Maxillary central incisors erupt at about 7-8 years, after the mandibular first molars and central incisors.
distractorExplanations.c: Second molars erupt at about 11-13 years and are called the 12-year molars, not the first permanent teeth.
distractorExplanations.d: Premolars erupt at about 10-12 years, replacing primary molars, well after the first permanent molars.

options.a: 5.5 (approximate)
options.b: 6.5 (approximate)
options.c: 7.0 (approximate)
options.d: 7.4 (approximate)

distractorExplanations.b: A critical pH of roughly 6.2-6.7 applies to root cementum and dentin, not to enamel, which holds until about 5.5.
distractorExplanations.c: pH 7.0 is neutral; enamel is stable there and does not begin to demineralize until about 5.5.
distractorExplanations.d: About 7.4 is blood pH and close to stimulated saliva; enamel is protected at that pH, not dissolving.

options.a: Produce collagen fibers that repair the attachment
options.b: Provide host defense against periodontal pathogens
options.c: Mineralize plaque into subgingival calculus deposits
options.d: Carry clotting factors that stop bleeding on probing

distractorExplanations.a: Collagen is produced by fibroblasts; leukocytes in crevicular fluid, mainly neutrophils, are defense cells.
distractorExplanations.c: Subgingival calculus mineralizes from minerals in crevicular fluid and serum; leukocytes do not calcify plaque.
distractorExplanations.d: Clotting depends on platelets and plasma proteins; leukocytes in crevicular fluid are immune cells.

options.a: Pulp irritation such as caries or trauma
options.b: Normal root completion after tooth eruption
options.c: Tooth development before the tooth erupts
options.d: Fluoride uptake from toothpaste over time

distractorExplanations.b: Dentin laid down physiologically after root completion is secondary dentin, not tertiary (reparative) dentin.
distractorExplanations.c: Dentin formed during development before root completion is primary dentin, not a response to injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Fluoride alters enamel and dentin mineral but does not trigger odontoblasts to form reparative dentin.

options.a: Sulcus/pocket depth from gingival margin to junctional epithelium
options.b: Clinical attachment level measured from the gingival margin
options.c: Gingival recession from the CEJ to the base of the pocket
options.d: Tooth mobility in millimeters, read by pressing with the probe tip alone

distractorExplanations.b: Clinical attachment level is referenced to the CEJ and calculated, not the direct probe reading from the margin.
distractorExplanations.c: Recession is CEJ to gingival margin; CEJ to the base of the pocket is clinical attachment level.
distractorExplanations.d: Mobility is assessed with two rigid instrument handles, not by pushing with a probe tip.

nbdhe-readiness-check-assessment-002.explanation: Probing depths assess periodontal pocketing as part of perio charting. The reading is an estimate of the attachment level.

options.a: Probing depth and the width of attached gingiva at each site
options.b: Probing depth and radiographic crestal bone height at each site
options.c: Gingival margin position and the mobility grade of each tooth
options.d: Probing depth and position of the gingival margin relative to the CEJ

distractorExplanations.a: Attached gingiva width is not part of the CAL calculation; CAL needs the margin position relative to the CEJ.
distractorExplanations.b: Radiographic bone height is a separate measure; CAL is a clinical measurement referenced to the CEJ.
distractorExplanations.c: Mobility is not part of CAL; the calculation needs probing depth plus margin position relative to the CEJ.

options.a: Incipient involvement; furcation felt but probe cannot enter it
options.b: Through-and-through bone loss, but the opening is covered by gingiva
options.c: Partial penetration into the furcation; probe does not pass through
options.d: Through-and-through bone loss with the furcation clinically visible

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a Class I furcation (Glickman), where the concavity is felt but not entered.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes Class III: the probe passes through, but soft tissue still covers the furcation entrance.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes Class IV: through-and-through loss with the furcation open to view because of recession.

options.a: Movement up to 1 mm in a facial-lingual direction
options.b: Severe mobility, often depressible in the socket
options.c: Movement greater than 1 mm, but not depressible
options.d: Normal physiologic movement within the PDL space

distractorExplanations.a: Movement up to about 1 mm is grade 1 (slight) mobility, not grade 3.
distractorExplanations.c: Movement over 1 mm without vertical depressibility is grade 2; grade 3 adds depressibility or severe movement.
distractorExplanations.d: Physiologic movement within the PDL space is grade 0, not severe grade 3 mobility.

options.a: Distance from gingival margin to the base of the sulcus or pocket
options.b: Distance from CEJ to the base of the pocket at the deepest site
options.c: Distance from gingival margin to the mucogingival junction
options.d: Distance from CEJ to gingival margin when margin is apical to CEJ

distractorExplanations.a: Margin to the base of the sulcus or pocket is probing depth, not recession.
distractorExplanations.b: CEJ to the base of the pocket is clinical attachment level, not recession.
distractorExplanations.c: Margin to the mucogingival junction is the width of keratinized gingiva, not recession.

options.a: Atrophy of filiform papillae leaving red migrating patches
options.b: Elongation of filiform papillae with pigment/debris
options.c: Candida overgrowth forming a wipeable white pseudomembrane
options.d: Enlargement of fungiform papillae from vitamin B deficiency

distractorExplanations.a: Loss of filiform papillae in red migrating patches is geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis).
distractorExplanations.c: A wipeable white pseudomembrane is pseudomembranous candidiasis, not elongated pigmented papillae.
distractorExplanations.d: B-vitamin deficiency causes atrophic glossitis with a smooth red tongue, not elongated dark filiform papillae.

options.a: Tooth vibration/mobility palpable under occlusal function
options.b: Tooth movement felt when pushed between two instrument handles
options.c: A rough, gritty sound heard over the TMJ during opening
options.d: Pain felt when the tooth is tapped with a mirror handle

distractorExplanations.b: That is the standard mobility test; fremitus is vibration felt while the patient taps or grinds the teeth.
distractorExplanations.c: A gritty TMJ sound during opening is crepitus, a joint finding, not tooth fremitus.
distractorExplanations.d: Pain on tapping is percussion sensitivity, which suggests periapical inflammation, not fremitus.

options.a: Assign the patient's caries risk level for recall and fluoride planning
options.b: Stage and grade the patient's periodontitis for the treatment plan
options.c: Estimate medical risk for dental care and need for modifications/consultation
options.d: Calculate the maximum local anesthetic dose from the patient's weight

distractorExplanations.a: Caries risk is assigned with tools such as CAMBRA; the ASA class rates systemic medical status.
distractorExplanations.b: Periodontitis staging and grading uses the 2017 AAP/EFP framework, not the ASA classification.
distractorExplanations.d: Maximum dose comes from body weight and the agent; the ASA class informs risk but is not a dose calculator.

options.a: Increased probing depth caused by apical migration of the junctional epithelium
options.b: Bone loss with an infrabony defect below the alveolar crest
options.c: Increased probing depth due to gingival enlargement without apical migration
options.d: Recession that exposes the root while probing depth stays shallow

distractorExplanations.a: Apical migration of the junctional epithelium creates a true periodontal pocket with attachment loss.
distractorExplanations.b: An infrabony defect is a true pocket with bone and attachment loss, not a gingival pseudopocket.
distractorExplanations.d: Recession moves the margin apically; a pseudopocket forms when enlarged gingiva moves the margin coronally.

nbdhe-readiness-check-assessment-011.explanation: Gingival hyperplasia can deepen sulci without true attachment loss. The attachment stays at its normal level.

options.a: A Gracey curet used as the main detection tool
options.b: A disclosing solution, which stains calculus dark red
options.c: Bitewing radiographs, which show all supragingival deposits
options.d: A periodontal probe and explorer with air drying

distractorExplanations.a: Curets are designed to remove deposits; explorers are the instruments designed for tactile detection.
distractorExplanations.b: Disclosing agents stain biofilm, not calculus reliably; calculus is found with air drying and an explorer.
distractorExplanations.c: Radiographs show mainly heavy interproximal calculus; supragingival deposits are detected clinically with air drying.

options.a: Reversible pulpitis from a new filling
options.b: Normal response of a healthy tooth
options.c: Possible periapical inflammation
options.d: Gingivitis limited to the papilla

distractorExplanations.a: Reversible pulpitis rarely causes pain on tapping; percussion pain reflects inflammation of the periapical tissues.
distractorExplanations.b: A healthy tooth with normal periapical tissues is not painful on percussion.
distractorExplanations.d: Gingivitis affects soft tissue only and does not cause pain when the tooth is tapped.

options.a: Reduce biofilm and calculus to resolve inflammation and facilitate healing
options.b: Remove all cementum to leave a glassy, smooth root surface for healing
options.c: Eliminate pockets surgically by excising the inflamed gingival wall of each pocket
options.d: Replace mechanical debridement with systemic antibiotics for most cases

distractorExplanations.b: Aggressive cementum removal is an outdated goal; modern debridement removes deposits while preserving cementum.
distractorExplanations.c: Excising the pocket wall is surgical therapy such as gingivectomy, not nonsurgical periodontal therapy.
distractorExplanations.d: Systemic antibiotics are adjuncts for selected cases; mechanical biofilm and calculus removal remains the core.

options.a: Effective calculus removal without water, which keeps the field drier for vision
options.b: Safe use on all patients, including those with unshielded older cardiac pacemakers
options.c: Lower aerosol production than hand scaling, so high-volume evacuation is unnecessary
options.d: Efficient calculus removal with lavage and less repetitive strain than hand scaling alone

distractorExplanations.a: Magnetostrictive and piezoelectric units need water coolant to prevent heat damage; they are not used dry.
distractorExplanations.b: Magnetostrictive units carry a caution for older unshielded pacemakers; device compatibility must be checked.
distractorExplanations.c: Ultrasonic scaling produces more aerosol than hand scaling; high-volume evacuation is recommended.

nbdhe-readiness-check-planning-impl-002.explanation: Power scalers remove deposits efficiently with irrigation; hand instruments still have roles. This holds in many cases.

options.a: They have a longer terminal shank, which is what limits them to deep pockets
options.b: They have one cutting edge offset for specific tooth surfaces
options.c: They have a pointed tip and triangular cross-section like a sickle
options.d: They have a face offset at 90 degrees for use on all tooth surfaces

distractorExplanations.a: Extended shanks are an After Five-type modification; area specificity comes from the offset single cutting edge.
distractorExplanations.c: A pointed tip and triangular cross-section describe a sickle scaler, not a curet of any kind.
distractorExplanations.d: A 90-degree face with two edges describes a universal curet; Graceys are offset about 60-70 degrees.

options.a: Generalized moderate pockets in place of scaling and root planing
options.b: Initial therapy, placed before any debridement to soften calculus
options.c: Shallow pockets of 3 mm or less that bleed on probing
options.d: Selected residual deep pockets after thorough debridement as adjuncts

distractorExplanations.a: Local delivery agents are adjuncts after debridement, not replacements for scaling and root planing.
distractorExplanations.b: Local antimicrobials are placed after thorough debridement into residual pockets; they do not soften calculus.
distractorExplanations.c: Local delivery is indicated for residual pockets of about 5 mm or more, not shallow 3 mm sites.

options.a: A sharp cutting edge for efficient calculus removal with less lateral pressure
options.b: The original face-to-lateral surface angle of 90 degrees on curets
options.c: A rounded edge that burnishes calculus smooth so it blends with the root surface
options.d: Instrument sterility, so sharpened curets can skip the autoclave

distractorExplanations.b: The curet face-to-lateral surface angle should be about 70-80 degrees; 90 degrees gives a dull, blunt edge.
distractorExplanations.c: Burnished calculus is a failure caused by dull instruments, not a goal of sharpening.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharpening does not sterilize; instruments are sharpened sterile and then reprocessed before use.

options.a: Polish every tooth at each visit with coarse paste to remove all stain
options.b: Polish only stained/plaque-retentive areas as needed
options.c: Polish implants with coarse pumice to remove stain
options.d: Polish only teeth that have calculus remaining after scaling

distractorExplanations.a: Routine full-mouth coarse polishing removes fluoride-rich surface enamel; selective polishing limits this.
distractorExplanations.c: Implants need nonabrasive or low-abrasive agents; coarse pumice scratches titanium and restorations.
distractorExplanations.d: Polishing does not remove calculus; selective polishing targets stain and plaque-retentive areas.

nbdhe-readiness-check-planning-impl-006.explanation: Evidence-based polishing is selective to preserve tooth structure/fluoride-rich enamel. This avoids unnecessary enamel removal.

options.a: Seal dentinal tubules permanently so desensitizers are not needed
options.b: Etch the enamel surface to prepare it for pit and fissure sealants
options.c: Disinfect pockets after scaling as a local antimicrobial agent
options.d: Aid remineralization and reduce sensitivity/caries risk when indicated

distractorExplanations.a: Varnish occlusion of tubules is temporary; it reduces sensitivity for a time but is not permanent.
distractorExplanations.b: Enamel is etched with phosphoric acid before sealants; fluoride varnish is not an etchant.
distractorExplanations.c: Fluoride varnish is not a pocket antimicrobial; local delivery agents such as chlorhexidine chips fill that role.

options.a: Ask the patient to leave the inhaler at home to avoid interactions with anesthetics
options.b: Ensure inhaler availability, reduce aerosols/stress, and confirm medical stability
options.c: Use air polishing and ultrasonic scaling freely, since aerosols help clear the airway
options.d: Premedicate with antibiotics before scaling, as asthma raises infection risk

distractorExplanations.a: The rescue inhaler must be at chairside; it does not interact with local anesthetic in a way that requires removal.
distractorExplanations.c: Aerosols and polishing powders can trigger bronchospasm in asthma; aerosol-generating steps are limited.
distractorExplanations.d: Asthma is not an indication for antibiotic prophylaxis; the focus is airway safety and medical stability.

options.a: Remove only the supragingival calculus so that the root surface is untouched
options.b: Excise the inflamed pocket lining epithelium so that a fresh connective tissue wound can heal
options.c: Remove calculus and endotoxin-contaminated cementum sufficiently to allow tissue healing
options.d: Create a glassy root surface by planing away the cementum layer down to dentin

distractorExplanations.a: Root planing addresses subgingival root surfaces; supragingival scaling alone is not root planing.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing the pocket lining is gingival curettage, a soft-tissue procedure, not root planing.
distractorExplanations.d: Planing away the cementum for a glassy surface is the outdated, overaggressive goal; modern planing is conservative.

nbdhe-readiness-check-planning-impl-009.explanation: Modern root planing focuses on deposit removal and biocompatible root surfaces, not aggressive cementum removal. This is the modern conservative approach.

options.a: Finer low-abrasive powders are less damaging to root surfaces/implants than traditional bicarb
options.b: Sodium bicarbonate powders are too fine to reach below the gingival margin at all
options.c: Glycine and erythritol have antibiotic action that replaces systemic antimicrobial therapy
options.d: Calcium carbonate powders are gentler, so glycine is chosen mainly for its flavor

distractorExplanations.b: The problem with sodium bicarbonate is that it is coarser and more abrasive, not that it is too fine.
distractorExplanations.c: Glycine and erythritol are low-abrasive powders, not antibiotics, and do not replace antimicrobial therapy.
distractorExplanations.d: Calcium carbonate is also an abrasive supragingival powder; glycine is chosen for its low abrasivity.

nbdhe-readiness-check-planning-impl-010.explanation: Low-abrasive powders support biofilm management with less root damage than coarse bicarb. This holds in many protocols.

options.a: Standardized, using one brushing method taught to every patient
options.b: Individualized, demonstrated, and evaluated for patient skill
options.c: Verbal only, since demonstrations can embarrass adult patients
options.d: Given once at the initial visit, then left to the patient at recalls

distractorExplanations.a: Instruction is tailored to the patient's dexterity, risks, and needs rather than one method for everyone.
distractorExplanations.c: Demonstration and return demonstration build skill; verbal instruction alone is less effective.
distractorExplanations.d: Instruction is reinforced and evaluated at every visit, not given once and dropped.

options.a: Confirm the needle has reached bone
options.b: Check that the anesthetic cartridge is not expired
options.c: Reduce risk of paresthesia from nerve contact
options.d: Reduce risk of intravascular injection

distractorExplanations.a: Bone contact is felt through the syringe; aspiration checks for blood to avoid intravascular injection.
distractorExplanations.b: Cartridge expiry is checked visually before loading; aspiration is about needle-tip position in a vessel.
distractorExplanations.c: Aspiration does not prevent nerve contact; paresthesia relates to needle trauma or the anesthetic agent.

options.a: Plastic curets, which leave resin residue on the implant
options.b: Titanium curets, which are softer than the implant abutment
options.c: Stainless steel curets that scratch titanium surfaces
options.d: Glycine air polishing, which is too abrasive for titanium

distractorExplanations.a: Plastic and resin instruments are recommended for implant maintenance because they do not scratch titanium.
distractorExplanations.b: Titanium curets match the implant's hardness and are recommended; they are not avoided.
distractorExplanations.d: Glycine powder is low-abrasive and is used around implants; it is not what should be avoided.

options.a: Increasing dentinal fluid flow so the pulp adapts to stimuli over time
options.b: Forming a resin bond layer the way a dentin bonding agent does
options.c: Occluding tubules or altering nerve excitability to reduce hypersensitivity
options.d: Sedating the pulp with anti-inflammatory action like eugenol

distractorExplanations.a: Under the hydrodynamic theory fluid movement causes the pain; desensitizers reduce flow rather than increase it.
distractorExplanations.b: Potassium nitrate and fluoride do not form a resin layer; that is how dentin bonding agents desensitize.
distractorExplanations.d: Eugenol is a sedative dressing material; potassium nitrate depolarizes nerve fibers and fluoride occludes tubules.

options.a: Biofilm control, professional debridement, and reevaluation
options.b: Scaling and root planing by quadrant with local anesthesia
options.c: Systemic antibiotics plus a chlorhexidine rinse for 6 months
options.d: Periodontal surgery referral when bleeding persists after one week

distractorExplanations.b: Quadrant scaling and root planing treats periodontitis; gingivitis has no attachment loss to root plane.
distractorExplanations.c: Systemic antibiotics are not indicated for plaque-induced gingivitis, and long-term chlorhexidine stains teeth.
distractorExplanations.d: Gingivitis is reversible with biofilm control and debridement; surgery is not part of its treatment plan.

options.a: Take a full-mouth radiograph series to confirm new bone fill in the treated pockets
options.b: Repeat full-mouth scaling and root planing on a fixed schedule
options.c: Assess tissue response and residual pocketing for further care decisions
options.d: Polish the teeth and apply sealants before the maintenance phase starts

distractorExplanations.a: Bone fill is not expected or assessed radiographically at reevaluation; tissue response is measured clinically.
distractorExplanations.b: Further instrumentation is limited to residual sites identified at reevaluation, not repeated full-mouth on schedule.
distractorExplanations.d: Reevaluation exists to measure the periodontal response; polishing and sealants do not serve that purpose.

options.a: Every 6 months, the same recall used for gingivitis patients
options.b: Individualized, often 3–4 months for periodontitis patients
options.c: Every 12 months once pockets have been reduced to 4 mm
options.d: Every 4–6 weeks for the first year after therapy

distractorExplanations.a: A 6-month recall suits many healthy or gingivitis patients; treated periodontitis usually needs about 3-4 months.
distractorExplanations.c: Annual intervals are too long for treated periodontitis; pathogens repopulate pockets within about 3 months.
distractorExplanations.d: Four to six weeks is the timing of the reevaluation visit after therapy, not the ongoing maintenance interval.

options.a: The diagnosis and procedure codes, with risks given only if the patient asks
options.b: Risks, benefits, alternatives, and expected outcomes in understandable language
options.c: Risks and benefits in technical terms so the record is legally precise
options.d: A signed form listing the procedure, with any alternatives left for the dentist to discuss

distractorExplanations.a: Material risks must be disclosed proactively; consent is not informed if risks wait for the patient to ask.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent requires language the patient understands; technical jargon undermines informed consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Alternatives, including no treatment, are a required element of the consent discussion, not an optional extra.

options.a: Acting legally if the supervising dentist gave verbal approval
options.b: Engaging in illegal practice that risks license and patient safety
options.c: Acting legally if the procedure is within ADHA's standards
options.d: Committing a billing violation that the insurer handles

distractorExplanations.a: A dentist's approval cannot expand hygiene scope beyond what the state practice act allows.
distractorExplanations.c: ADHA standards are professional guidance; the legal scope of practice is set by the state practice act.
distractorExplanations.d: Practicing outside scope is a licensure and legal violation handled by the state board, not an insurer billing issue.

options.a: Share PHI only for treatment/payment/operations or with authorization as permitted
options.b: Share PHI with family members who ask, as long as they live with the patient
options.c: Withhold the patient's own records unless a court orders their release
options.d: Post patient photos online once the name has been cropped from the image

distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA requires the patient's agreement or a chance to object before sharing with family; living together is not enough.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients have a HIPAA right of access to their own records; no court order is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Facial photos are identifiers under HIPAA; posting them needs written authorization even without a name.

options.a: A population-level caries prevention measure supported by public health evidence
options.b: A measure mainly for children that offers adults little caries benefit
options.c: A systemic measure that works mainly through pre-eruptive uptake into developing enamel
options.d: A measure set at 1.5 mg/L, the current U.S. recommended level

distractorExplanations.b: Fluoridation benefits all ages, including reducing coronal and root caries in adults.
distractorExplanations.c: Fluoridation's benefit is now attributed mainly to frequent low-level topical exposure after eruption.
distractorExplanations.d: The U.S. Public Health Service recommendation has been 0.7 mg/L since 2015, not 1.5 mg/L.

options.a: Slight wear on the occlusal surface of the sealant
options.b: Sealant discoloration without any marginal gap
options.c: A sealant that looks opaque white rather than clear
options.d: Partial/complete loss or catch with explorer

distractorExplanations.a: Minor occlusal wear is expected; retention is judged by material loss or a marginal catch.
distractorExplanations.b: Surface staining with sealed margins is not retention failure; an explorer catch or loss is.
distractorExplanations.c: Many sealants are opaque white by design so they are easy to check; color is not a failure sign.

nbdhe-readiness-check-eval-ethics-007.explanation: Lost or leaking sealants need repair to restore protection. Either finding indicates the need for repair or replacement.

options.a: Adapting communication and care respectfully to patient cultural needs
options.b: Using family members as interpreters to save time and cost
options.c: Applying one standard script to every patient so that no cultural bias can enter care
options.d: Assuming a patient's beliefs from their ethnic background

distractorExplanations.b: Trained medical interpreters are preferred; family interpreters risk errors and privacy problems.
distractorExplanations.c: A uniform script ignores individual cultural and language needs; competence means adapting care respectfully.
distractorExplanations.d: Inferring beliefs from ethnicity is stereotyping; culturally competent care asks and adapts to the individual.

options.a: Disease present, test negative
options.b: Disease absent, test negative
options.c: Disease absent, test positive
options.d: Disease present, test positive

distractorExplanations.c: A positive test in a person without disease is a false positive, not a true negative.
distractorExplanations.a: False negative.
distractorExplanations.d: True positive.

options.a: DMFT/DMFS
options.b: deft/defs
options.c: CPITN/CPI
options.d: OHI-S

distractorExplanations.b: Lowercase deft/defs indexes record caries experience in primary teeth, not permanent teeth.
distractorExplanations.c: CPITN and CPI measure periodontal status and treatment needs, not caries experience.
distractorExplanations.d: The Simplified Oral Hygiene Index scores debris and calculus, not caries experience in permanent teeth.

options.a: Explain rationale/risks of refusal, document, and inform the dentist
options.b: Have the patient sign a waiver so radiographs are no longer required
options.c: Proceed with treatment and skip documenting the refusal
options.d: Dismiss the patient from the practice at once for noncompliance

distractorExplanations.b: A refusal form documents informed refusal but does not remove the diagnostic need or the dentist's judgment.
distractorExplanations.c: An informed refusal must be documented in the record, with the risks explained to the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Dismissal is not the first response; the hygienist educates, documents, and informs the dentist.

nbdhe-readiness-check-eval-ethics-011.explanation: Respect autonomy with informed refusal and appropriate care adjustments. Care is then modified as needed.

options.a: Asking how often the patient brushes and flosses each day
options.b: Counting restorations placed since the last recall visit
options.c: Radiographic bone levels compared with the prior series
options.d: Plaque scores/disclosing and skill demonstration review

distractorExplanations.a: Self-reported frequency tends to overstate hygiene; plaque scores and skill review measure actual effectiveness.
distractorExplanations.b: Restoration counts reflect past caries treatment, not how well the patient is currently removing biofilm.
distractorExplanations.c: Bone level changes are a slow periodontal outcome, not a measure of current oral hygiene effectiveness.

options.a: Report to police in every case, even if the adult patient objects
options.b: Follow state reporting laws, document objectively, and provide resources/referrals
options.c: Document the patient's statements in the chart but leave out any injury findings you observed
options.d: Confront the suspected partner privately in the operatory to clarify the situation

distractorExplanations.a: Many states do not mandate reporting adult intimate partner violence; the hygienist follows that state's law.
distractorExplanations.c: Objective findings such as injury location, size, and appearance are central to the record.
distractorExplanations.d: Confronting the suspected abuser can escalate danger to the patient; referral and resources are the safe route.

nbdhe-readiness-check-eval-ethics-014.explanation: Safety, documentation, legal mandates, and resources guide response. Act per office protocol.

options.a: Reduced BOP, improved attachment/probing trends, and controllable biofilm
options.b: Radiographic bone fill visible at the first reevaluation visit
options.c: Absence of patient-reported pain at the maintenance visit
options.d: Complete calculus removal at the visit, confirmed by careful tactile exploring

distractorExplanations.b: Bone fill is not the expected outcome of nonsurgical therapy; success is judged by bleeding and probing trends.
distractorExplanations.c: Periodontitis is often painless, so a lack of pain says little about disease control.
distractorExplanations.d: Deposit removal is the means; success is the tissue response, measured by bleeding and attachment trends.
